reason: The case study quote states the company has reduced database management cost by five times since migrating to Amazon RDS.

The history row dated November 20, 2024 states blue/green deployments can adjust storage settings in the green environment.

The db.t4g quote says instances can burst beyond the baseline over a 24-hour window for an additional charge; the claim drops the over-a-24-hour-window qualifier. The db.t3 part is supported.
The quote states balanced compute, memory and networking only for db.m7g; the claim generalises it to all db.m general-purpose classes.

The quotes support db.z1d as optimized for memory-intensive applications and db.x1 as one of the lowest price per GiB of RAM; neither quote says the db.x families are optimized for memory-intensive applications.
Under the db.t2 bullet the quote states AWS recommends these classes only for development and test servers, or other non-production servers.
The quotes introduce general-purpose, memory-optimized, compute-optimized and burstable-performance class lists; no quote mentions Optimized Reads classes.
The quote states RDS sends metrics to CloudWatch every minute for each active database with no additional charges for RDS metrics.
Under basic operational guidelines the quote states use metrics for memory, CPU, replica lag and storage, with CloudWatch notifications on pattern change or approaching capacity limits.
The comparison row states non-Aurora Multi-AZ: only the primary instance is active; read replicas: all accessible and usable for read scaling.
The comparison row states non-Aurora Multi-AZ automated backups are taken from standby and read replicas have no backups configured by default.
The comparison row states non-Aurora Multi-AZ upgrades happen on primary and non-Aurora read replica upgrades are independent from the source instance.
The row says a non-Aurora read replica can be manually promoted to a standalone instance; it does not say promotion must be manual, so the claim's must is stronger than the quote.
The comparison row states Single-AZ risks data loss and hours of failover, one standby fails over automatically to the up-to-date standby, and one of two remaining standbys takes over writes.
